title: HIV Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) within 72 Hours
sourceOrganization: World Health Organization (WHO) & Ethiopian Federal Ministry of Health (FMoH)
summary: PEP is a 28-day course of antiretroviral medicines taken strictly within 72 hours of potential HIV exposure to prevent infection.
keyPoints: Must be started within 72 hours of exposure (ideally within 2 to 24 hours).
Available free and confidentially at public Hospital Emergency Departments and Woreda Health Centers in Ethiopia.
Requires taking antiretroviral medications daily without interruption for 28 consecutive days.
Baseline and follow-up HIV testing at 4 to 6 weeks and 3 months is essential.
detailedContent: Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) is an emergency medical response to potential HIV exposure (unprotected sex, condom rupture, sexual violence, or accidental needle-stick).
In Ethiopia, public hospitals operate 24/7 emergency desks and specialized One-Stop Centers where PEP medications (Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Dolutegravir) are provided free of charge.
Adherence to the complete 28-day regimen is critical; stopping early significantly diminishes protective efficacy.
whenToSeeClinician: Seek clinical evaluation at an emergency department or health center immediately. Every hour counts; do not delay beyond 72 hours.
ethiopiaContext: Free of charge at all Ethiopian public health centers and hospital emergency wards under national HIV guidelines.

title: HIV Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) for Prevention
sourceOrganization: Ethiopian Federal Ministry of Health (FMoH) & UNAIDS
summary: PrEP is daily medicine taken by individuals at ongoing risk of HIV to decrease transmission risk by over 99%.
keyPoints: Taken daily by HIV-negative individuals who have ongoing risk of HIV exposure.
Reduces sexual transmission risk by >99% when taken consistently.
Does not protect against pregnancy or other STIs (syphilis, gonorrhea, chlamydia); combine with condoms for dual protection.
Requires kidney function screening and regular HIV testing every 3 months.
detailedContent: Oral PrEP (TDF/FTC) creates a preventive shield in genital tissues preventing HIV from establishing viral infection.
PrEP is offered in Ethiopia at designated ART clinics, drop-in centers, and youth-friendly reproductive health sites.
Condoms must still be used alongside PrEP to safeguard against other STIs and unintended pregnancy.
whenToSeeClinician: Visit your local health center or Marie Stopes clinic to receive confidential counseling, kidney safety screening, and a PrEP starter kit.
ethiopiaContext: Scaled nationwide in Ethiopia across high-burden urban corridors, university health clinics, and key populations.

title: Undetectable = Untransmittable (U=U) and Viral Suppression
summary: People living with HIV on regular antiretroviral therapy (ART) with undetectable viral loads cannot transmit HIV to sexual partners.
keyPoints: U=U means Undetectable = Untransmittable.
When viral load remains under 200 copies/mL for at least 6 months, transmission risk via sex is zero.
Daily adherence to ART maintains maternal health and enables HIV-serodiscordant couples to have healthy children.
Routine viral load testing every 6 to 12 months confirms continued suppression.
detailedContent: Decades of clinical trials have confirmed that consistent ART suppresses the virus to levels undetectable by standard laboratory assays.
This scientific truth transforms lives by eliminating stigma, restoring reproductive confidence, and supporting healthy sexual relationships.
whenToSeeClinician: If on ART, schedule your 6-month viral load check at your local health center ART clinic to verify suppression.
ethiopiaContext: Adopted by the Ethiopian Ministry of Health in national viral suppression and stigma-reduction guidelines.

title: HIV Testing Types and Window Periods
summary: Explains antibody, antigen/antibody combo, and nucleic acid tests and the biological window period after potential exposure.
keyPoints: The window period is the interval between HIV exposure and when a test can reliably detect infection.
Rapid antibody fingerstick tests: detect antibodies 23 to 90 days post-exposure.
4th-generation antigen/antibody lab tests: detect p24 antigen as early as 18 to 45 days.
A negative test during the window period should always be repeated at 12 weeks for conclusive verification.
detailedContent: Draft overview on HIV self-testing (HIVST) oral kits (OraQuick) available at retail pharmacies in Addis Ababa, Hawassa, and Adama.
Pending clinical verification for updated Ethiopian National HIV Testing Algorithm 2026 updates.
whenToSeeClinician: Consult a voluntary counseling and testing (VCT) counselor or visit your health center if exposed within the last 12 weeks.
ethiopiaContext: Self-testing oral swab kits are being expanded across urban pharmacies in Ethiopia.

title: Adolescent Confidential HIV Testing & Youth-Friendly Services (YFS)
sourceOrganization: Ethiopian Federal Ministry of Health (FMoH) - National Adolescent & Youth Health Strategy
summary: Under Ethiopian national policy, adolescents (including 15-year-olds) have the full legal right to access confidential HIV counseling, testing, and care at public health centers without parental consent.
keyPoints: Confidential & Without Parental Consent: The Ethiopian National Adolescent and Youth Health Strategy guarantees young people access to confidential Youth-Friendly Services (YFS) at public health facilities without parental notification or permission.
Dedicated Youth-Friendly Corners: Public health centers feature specialized YFS corners staffed by counselors trained in stigma-free, non-judgmental adolescent care.
Free Rapid Testing: Testing is conducted using a simple, gentle fingerstick rapid test that delivers accurate, confidential results in 15 to 20 minutes.
Testing Window Period: Rapid antibody tests detect infection between 3 and 12 weeks post-exposure; a negative result within this window should be confirmed with a follow-up test at 12 weeks.
detailedContent: Adolescents frequently avoid essential healthcare out of fear that parents or community members will find out. Ethiopian national guidelines strictly protect youth patient privacy.
Providers are prohibited from disclosing testing status, sexual history, or service usage to family members or third parties without the adolescent's explicit consent.
whenToSeeClinician: Visit the Youth-Friendly Service (YFS) corner at your nearest public health center or call Marie Stopes toll-free (8044) for free, confidential, stigma-free HIV counseling and testing.
ethiopiaContext: Confidential YFS corners operational across public health centers in all Ethiopian regional states; no parental consent required.
